text.p: For months Japan and the U.S. have been trying to fine-tune the dollar/yen exchange rate, and the market may now be close to a level which would satisfy both countries, analysts said.
The problem is volatility, with the dollar recently seeing moves of up to five yen in one day -- a nightmare for the monetary authorities.

The dollar, after rising steadily on the back of a robust U.S. economy to a 55-month peak of 127.47 yen on May 1, had slid about 10 percent, or 12 yen, from that level by Thursday. At 1430 GMT the dollar stood at 116.30 yen.

"We're probably at that level now where the U.S. and Japan are happy, they're just probably not happy with the speed of the move," said Paul Lambert, senior currency economist at UBS. "If the market will now trade in an orderly fashion, everyone would probably be satisfied."
Japan has been the country most concerned about exchange rates during the dollar/yen's recent bumpy ride and hence the one providing the constant stream of verbal intervention.
Analysts said Japanese officials' recent comments urging calm in the market showed they did not want the dollar to fall further.

"They're trying to calm the dollar, saying 'it's gone far enough, thank you very much'... I think they're quite happy with dollar/yen where it is currently," said Nigel Richardson, international economist at Yamaichi International.
Dollar/yen traded around 116.35 yen in European afternoon trade on Thursday after earlier tumbling to 114.70, its lowest since late December, versus 117.97 yen in late European trading on Wednesday.

Japan would rather avoid a strong yen since the currency's strength in the past few years has battered its crucial exporting industry, but officials had become increasingly vociferous in their concern about the weakening yen as the dollar neared its 55-month peak.
Analysts said the dollar plunge this week has given Japan more than it bargained for, and it is now doing an about-turn.
The U.S., for its part, has been far less nervous about currency moves and is unlikely to be perturbed by the dollar's recent slide, analysts said.
While Washington has stressed a strong dollar is in its interest, as far as dollar/yen is concerned it is worried a weak yen would swell its huge trade deficit with Japan.

Driving the dollar's tumble overnight was speculation the U.S. would support a stronger yen, fuelled by talk Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin was calling for a dollar/yen rate of 115 in a newsletter from a U.S. consulting firm.
Analysts said this led to a market consensus around 115 yen or slightly below which was likely to keep authorities happy on both sides of the Pacific.
"The Japanese don't want a really strong yen because of their export industry," said Adrian Davies, senior strategist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull in London.
"So basically there is a comfort zone both the U.S. and Japan would be happy with, and when the dollar gets down to around 115 yen, the Japanese say 'no more'," Davies said.
This did indeed seem to be the case on Thursday.

Top officials at Japan's Finance Ministry, including minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, said recent currency moves showed the Group of Seven finance ministers' message, sent through a communique after their April meeting, had now "fully" filtered through into the market.
The G7 communique said it was undesirable for exchange rates to deviate from fundamentals, and stressed the need to avoid rates which could lead to large trade imbalances.

Meanwhile, some analysts said there might be a turnaround in the market's perception of central bank intervention. Whereas in recent weeks fears centred on central bank dollar-selling, the U.S. currency's recent nosedive may raise the spectre of dollar buying by the authorities.

"You can't rule out the chance of intervention to support dollar/yen," UBS's Lambert said. "One thing central banks agree on is that intervention should be used to restore order to markets. I think they would come in if the market became what they see as disorderly."
